title: Finding the right pathway is the key to success
case_prompt:
A 24‐year‐old woman was referred for management of recurrent, hemodynamically tolerated broad‐complex tachycardia consistent with right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) ventricular tachycardia (VT). Over the preceding 3 months, she had been hospitalized 10 times for symptomatic palpitations, requiring several direct current cardioversions. She had no family history of premature sudden cardiac death.  
Initial investigations included a normal echocardiogram, a normal 12‐lead electrocardiogram, and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showing only minor irregularities in the free wall of the right ventricle. A 24‐hour Holter monitor revealed a high burden of ventricular ectopy correlating with her symptoms. She was treated sequentially with bisoprolol, diltiazem, and sotalol without satisfactory control.  
Two prior elective catheter ablations were performed using 3D mapping, both localizing the earliest activation to the RVOT. Radiofrequency ablation during VT termination was achieved each time, but inducibility of the clinical VT persisted, and no endocardial scar or diastolic pathway was identified.  
On referral to our center, flecainide was initiated. A new 12‐lead ECG demonstrated T‐wave inversion in leads V₁–V₃, contrasting with her previous normal repolarization. An exercise ECG reproduced VT of similar morphology at a slightly slower rate. The repolarization changes and resistance to endocardial ablation prompted reevaluation, and an electrophysiology study was scheduled.  
At the start of the procedure, VT was easily induced with a 600‐ms drive and an S2 at 320 ms from the right ventricular apex. Three‐dimensional endocardial mapping again localized the earliest activation to the septal RVOT, and radiofrequency ablation at this site terminated VT after 20 seconds. Consolidation lesions were delivered, but VT remained inducible with the same protocol.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Idiopathic focal RVOT VT was initially favored because “VT with left bundle branch block morphology and an inferior axis is often caused by focal tachycardia arising from the RVOT.”  
2. The absence of endocardial scar or diastolic pathway on prior mapping argued against a macroreentrant substrate such as ARVC: “neither endocardial scar nor a diastolic pathway was seen during either study.”  
3. The new repolarization changes and failure of endocardial ablation raised suspicion for ARVC, meeting Task Force Criteria: “The repolarization changes seen on the 12-lead ECG and the resistance of the arrhythmia to endocardial ablation prompted a reevaluation of the diagnosis… given the borderline diagnosis comprised of 1 major (12-lead ECG TWI) and 1 minor criteria (VT with inferior axis).”
